gaps.fact: Base spirit, mixers and garnish of the Aviation: never named anywhere in the Codex (no chapter, stem or service row). The usual spec: gin, maraschino liqueur, lemon juice and crème de violette, garnished with a cherry or a lemon twist.

Base spirit, mixers and garnish of the French Martini: never named anywhere in the Codex (no chapter, stem or service row). The usual spec: vodka, black raspberry liqueur and pineapple juice, shaken, a lemon twist.

Base spirit, mixers and garnish of the Greyhound: never named anywhere in the Codex (no chapter, stem or service row). The usual spec: vodka (or gin) and grapefruit juice over ice; with a salted rim it becomes a Salty Dog.

Base spirit, mixers and garnish of the John Collins: never named anywhere in the Codex (no chapter, stem or service row). The usual spec: the Collins built on whiskey, usually bourbon, with lemon, sugar and soda, a lemon slice and a cherry; older recipes used genever.
Base spirit, mixers and garnish of the Kamikaze: never named anywhere in the Codex (no chapter, stem or service row). The usual spec: vodka, triple sec and lime juice, shaken, a lime wedge.

Base spirit, mixers and garnish of the Pimm's Cup: never named anywhere in the Codex (no chapter, stem or service row). The usual spec: Pimm's No. 1 lengthened with lemonade or ginger ale, with cucumber, mint and fruit as the garnish.

errors.where: js/data-service-ref.js, SERVICE_REF tables cocktails, row Sazerac: '60 ml rye whiskey (the original took Cognac)'; and service question s-ukib3ha3, explanation: 'The Sazerac is rye (Cognac in the original)'
errors.claim: The original Sazerac was made with Cognac.
errors.correction: Say the drink is said to have first been made with Cognac, or that recipes on both spirits survive. The Codex's own Village question c-0dyutx4m says the name comes from a Cognac brand once sold in the city and that the brandy to rye story after phylloxera is a tradition rather than a documented fact; the service table and s-ukib3ha3 state as fact what c-0dyutx4m rightly calls undocumented, so the two parts of the Codex disagree.
errors.source: The Codex's own explanation of c-0dyutx4m; the drink's printed history, whose earliest recorded recipes do not settle a Cognac original

notes: Mapped questions: Village 54 (Spirits & Cocktails, of which 6 are on cocktails: the Sazerac c-0dyutx4m, the 1806 definition c-frr4eljb, stirring against shaking c-23lu2dp2, dilution c-zqvmp4vu, the highball family c-8cd2bcqh and the Last Word c-hx74ojnt, which is not on the Court's list); no Régionale door, since the subject is Certified only, though the Régionale Sake & Spirits stem i-hf81bjf8 asks the Negroni's Campari. Of the Court's 33 cocktails, 2 are asked by a stem in either bank (Negroni, Sazerac), 6 more are taught in the Village chapter's stirred and shaken classics (Daiquiri, Manhattan, Margarita, Old Fashioned, Sidecar, Whiskey Sour), 16 more appear only in the serviceRef cocktails table, and 9 are never named (Aviation, French Martini, Greyhound, John Collins, Kamikaze, Pimm's Cup, Rusty Nail, Sea Breeze, White Russian). Three serviceRef questions outside both banks (s-ukib3ha3, s-2c27f7pg, s-h5dxuen2) ask the Sazerac's bitters, the Negroni and the Kir Royale. The Court asks base spirits, mixers and garnishes, never measures or method, so an e- question per drink should key one of those three and leave the measures to the table. The table spells the Court's Whiskey Sour as Whisky Sour while building it on bourbon; it is the same drink. The table's specs (Mai Tai, Vesper, Vieux Carré, French 75, Champagne Cocktail, Gimlet, Pisco Sour) were read against the classic recipes and hold. No law or classification governs these drinks; no search was spent.
